intro: A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output, like a machine. This branch teaches how to write, read, graph and combine functions, which is the language most of higher math is written in.

IV.2.01.what: Using the shorthand f(x), read "f of x", to mean the output of rule f when the input is x.

levels.a: Explains in words what a statement like f(7) = 8 means.
levels.b: Tells apart finding an output, f(3), from finding the input that gives 3.
levels.c: Writes real situations, like the cost of 10 rides, in this shorthand.
levels.d: Writes a function rule from a description in words.
levels.e: Works backwards from a rule written in a disguised form to find the plain rule.
levels.f: Untangles two linked equations about the same function to find one of its outputs.

IV.2.02.what: Evaluating a function: putting a given input into the rule and working out the output.

levels.a: Puts whole numbers into a rule and works out the result.
levels.b: Puts in negative numbers and fractions.
levels.c: Puts in a whole expression, like a + 1, and simplifies what comes out.
levels.d: Reads outputs off a graph or a table instead of a formula.
levels.e: Uses one known output to find a missing number in the rule, then evaluates.
levels.f: Builds outputs up one step at a time from a rule that refers to the previous output.

IV.2.03.what: Finding a function's domain (all inputs allowed) and range (all outputs it can produce).

levels.a: Lists the inputs and outputs from a set of number pairs.
levels.b: Reads the domain and range off a graph.
levels.c: Finds inputs to exclude from a formula, such as those causing division by zero or square roots of negatives.
levels.d: Writes the domain and range as ranges in bracket form.
levels.e: Finds the domain when two restrictions apply at once.
levels.f: Finds the range of a trickier rule, where a clever idea is needed.

IV.2.04.what: Reading information from the graph of a function, such as outputs, solutions and where two graphs meet.

levels.a: Reads an output from a graph at a given input.
levels.b: Finds every input on a graph that gives a chosen output.
levels.c: Uses two graphs to find where one lies above the other.
levels.d: Reads the points where two graphs cross.
levels.e: Solves equations where the input has been doubled or shifted, still using the graph.
levels.f: Applies a graphed function twice in a row and finds every input that lands on a given value.

IV.2.05.what: Understanding what a function means in a real situation, such as cost depending on number of rides.

levels.a: Names what the input and the output stand for.
levels.b: Explains a statement like C(10) = 50 in plain words.
levels.c: Decides which inputs make sense in the situation, such as no negative time.
levels.d: Gives the units of inputs, outputs and rates, such as dollars per ride.

IV.2.06.what: Finding the average rate of change: how much the output changes for each one-unit change in input, over a stretch.

levels.a: Computes change in output divided by change in input using a formula.
levels.b: Finds the average rate of change from a table of values.
levels.d: Explains what the rate means in context, such as liters drained per minute.

IV.2.07.what: Identifying where a graph goes up (increasing), goes down (decreasing), or stays flat as you read left to right.

levels.a: Spots whether a graph rises or falls over a given stretch.
levels.b: Writes the rising and falling stretches as ranges of x.
levels.c: Finds stretches where the graph stays flat.
levels.d: Links rising to a positive rate of change and falling to a negative one.

IV.2.08.what: Finding where a graph crosses the axes: the y-intercept, and the zeros (inputs that give an output of zero).

levels.a: Finds where the graph crosses the vertical axis by putting in zero.
levels.b: Finds the zeros of a simple straight-line rule.
levels.c: Reads the zeros and the crossing point off a graph.
levels.d: Finds the zeros of a curved rule using algebra.

IV.2.09.what: Finding the highest and lowest points of a graph, either nearby peaks and valleys or the overall top and bottom.

levels.a: Tells whether a point is a local peak, a local valley, or neither.
levels.b: Finds the overall highest and lowest values of a whole graph.
levels.c: Reads a minimum or maximum value and where it happens from a graph.
levels.d: Explains what a maximum means in context, such as the best price for profit.

IV.2.10.what: Working with piecewise functions, which use different rules for different ranges of input, like tax brackets.

levels.a: Chooses the right rule for a given input and evaluates it.
levels.b: Matches each piece to its part of the graph.
levels.c: Reads filled and open dots to tell which piece owns a boundary point.
levels.d: Writes each piece's rule from a graph.

IV.2.11.what: Working with step functions, whose graphs look like stairs, such as parking fees charged per started hour.

levels.a: Rounds numbers down or up to a whole number using the floor and ceiling rules.
levels.b: Matches a step rule to its staircase graph.
levels.c: Solves postage and parking problems charged per started unit.
levels.d: Works out the value exactly at a jump and just after it.
levels.e: Works backwards from a step output to find all the inputs that give it.
levels.f: Solves puzzle equations that mix a number with its rounded-down value.

IV.2.12.what: Working with the absolute value function, whose graph is a V shape.

levels.a: Matches V-shaped graphs to their equations.
levels.b: Finds the tip of the V and the steepness of each side.
levels.c: Rewrites the V as two straight-line pieces.
levels.d: Solves equations by seeing where the V meets a flat line.

IV.2.13.what: Combining two functions by adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing their outputs.

levels.a: Adds two functions' outputs at a given input.
levels.b: Subtracts one function from another and simplifies.
levels.c: Multiplies or divides two functions and simplifies.
levels.d: Finds which inputs are allowed after combining, avoiding division by zero.
levels.e: Works backwards from a sum and a difference to recover the original functions.
levels.f: Splits a function into a mirror-symmetric part and a flip-symmetric part.

IV.2.14.what: Composition: feeding the output of one function straight into another, like two machines in a row.

levels.a: Applies one function, then the other, to a number.
levels.b: Writes the combined rule as a single expression.
levels.c: Shows that doing the two functions in the other order usually gives a different result.
levels.d: Breaks a complicated rule into an inside function and an outside function.
levels.e: Finds a missing number so that both orders give the same result.
levels.f: Applies a function hundreds of times by spotting that the results repeat in a cycle.

IV.2.15.what: Finding the inverse of a function: the rule that undoes it, taking each output back to its input.

levels.a: Describes in words the steps that undo a function, in reverse order.
levels.b: Finds the inverse rule by swapping x and y and solving.
levels.c: Sees the inverse's graph as a mirror image across the diagonal line y = x.
levels.d: Checks whether two functions undo each other.
